---
title: "Quiz: FLIM-FRET and metabolic imaging"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. 80 MHz: ω = 0.503 rad/ns.

---

**Q1.** Why does FRET shorten the donor's lifetime?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The lifetime is one over the total rate of leaving the excited state.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Transfer to the acceptor is an extra way to leave the excited state. More exits, higher total rate, shorter mean waiting time: $1/\tau_{DA} = 1/\tau_D + k_T$.
:::

---

**Q2.** The donor alone has τ = 2.5 ns; with the acceptor 1.5 ns. What is E, and which distance does it suggest for $R_0 = 5$ nm?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$E = 1 - \tau_{DA}/\tau_D$; $r = R_0(1/E - 1)^{1/6}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
E = 1 − 1.5/2.5 = 0.4. $r = 5 \cdot 1.5^{1/6} = 5.35$ nm.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why does lifetime-based FRET not need the bleed-through and cross-excitation corrections of intensity-based FRET?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which molecule's light is measured?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Only the donor's decay is recorded, and its lifetime does not depend on how many donors or acceptors there are. Intensity FRET compares channels whose values depend on concentrations, bleed-through and cross-excitation, which must be measured and subtracted.
:::

---

**Q4.** 30 % of the donors interact, at E = 0.6 ($\tau_D$ = 2.5 ns). Where on the line from the donor point to the FRET point does the pixel's phasor lie?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Position = photon fraction; photons per molecule ∝ lifetime.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\tau_{DA} = 1.0$ ns. Photon fraction $f = 0.3 \cdot 1.0/(0.3 \cdot 1.0 + 0.7 \cdot 2.5) = 0.15$: only 15 % of the way from the donor point, although 30 % of the molecules interact.
:::

---

**Q5.** Two experiments give the same mean donor lifetime. Could the interaction still be different? How would you tell?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Efficiency and fraction.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Yes: all donors at a low efficiency, or fewer donors at a high efficiency, can give the same mean lifetime (with τ_D = 2.5 ns: all at E = 0.3, or 71 % at E = 0.6, both 1.75 ns). A bi-exponential fit with $\tau_D$ fixed, or the phasor plot, separates them: the first lies on the semicircle, the second inside it, on the line from the donor point.
:::

---

**Q6.** Free NADH (0.4 ns) and bound NADH (2.5 ns): a cell's phasor lies 40 % of the way from free to bound. Is 40 % of its NADH bound?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Photon fraction vs molecule fraction.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No, 40 % of the **photons** come from bound NADH. Per molecule, bound NADH gives about 2.5/0.4 = 6 times more photons (assuming the same radiative rate), so the molecule fraction is $(0.4/2.5)/(0.4/2.5 + 0.6/0.4) = 0.10$.
:::

---

**Q7.** A FRET pixel's phasor lies outside the semicircle. What could cause that?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which kind of decay has a phasor outside the semicircle?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A component that **rises** before it decays: acceptor emission leaking into the donor channel (it is excited through FRET, so it lags behind). Its phasor is the product $P_{DA}P_A$, outside the semicircle. Noise or a wrong calibration can also push points just outside.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that the amplitude-weighted mean lifetime of a population with interacting fraction α and efficiency E is $\tau_D(1 - \alpha E)$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\bar\tau_a = (1 - \alpha)\tau_D + \alpha\tau_{DA}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\bar\tau_a = (1 - \alpha)\tau_D + \alpha\tau_D(1 - E) = \tau_D(1 - \alpha E)$. So $1 - \bar\tau_a/\tau_D = \alpha E$: the "apparent efficiency" from the amplitude-weighted mean is the product of fraction and efficiency, and cannot separate them.
:::
